| @StaplesEtAl2013 | TOEFL iBT written responses (N = 480) | Three proficiency levels | Lower-rated responses used more bundles overall and more prompt-identical bundles; functional distribution similar across levels |

## Proficiency and phraseological development

A distinct strand of bundle research asks not how learners differ from native speakers but how learner phraseology changes as proficiency develops, holding the task constant and varying rated proficiency. @ChenBaker2016 tracked lexical bundles in learner essays rated at CEFR levels B1, B2 and C1, showing that bundle repertoires discriminate across proficiency levels, with lower-rated essays leaning disproportionately on a small set of high-frequency frames and higher-rated essays approximating the wider, more register-appropriate repertoire of expert academic prose. Assessment data complicate any assumption that more bundles signal higher proficiency: in TOEFL iBT writing responses, @StaplesEtAl2013 found that lower-rated writers used more bundles overall, including more bundles reproduced from the prompts themselves, while the functional distribution of bundles remained broadly similar across levels. Development, on this evidence, is not an accumulation of sequences but a redistribution: what changes with proficiency is which frames are preferred, what functions they serve, and how closely they track the norms of the target register.

This picture of phraseological development as conditioned by register aligns with the complexity findings reviewed in Section 3.2, where phrasal complexity rose and clausal complexity fell across levels of study in BAWE [@StaplesEtAl2016], and where both proficiency and task type predicted lexico-grammatical profiles in TOEFL iBT data [@BiberGrayStaples2016]. For the present thesis, the strand licenses treating proficiency as a conditioning variable rather than a nuisance factor: where proficiency information is available, phraseological differences must be read against it before they are attributed to L1 background or to register. It also leaves open the question taken up in Section 4.8, whether the developmental patterns established for institutional writing hold at all in the informal, public registers that institutional corpora have not sampled.

## What existing L2 stance and phraseology research does not tell us

The field surveyed in this section can be summarised in terms of what is now reasonably well established. L2 writers differ from native writers in the deployment of stance, most relibaly in the calibration of epistemic commitment: a restricted range of devices, stronger and less precisely graded commitments, and coexisiting patterns of over- and undermarking [@HylandMilton1997; @Hinkel2005; @Adel2006; @BaxNakatsuharaWaller2019]. Stance changes developmentally, toward delimited, dialogically aware positioning [@AullLancaster2014; @CrosthwaiteJiang2017]. Differences between learner and native-speaker writing appear in recurrent multi-word sequences as well as in individual items: in bundle range, structural type and functional distribution [@ChenBaker2010; @AdelErman2012; @BychkovskaLee2017]. And phraseological repertoires vary systematically with both proficiency and register [@ChenBaker2016; @BiberBarbieri2007; @Hyland2008].

What this literature does not tell us equally clear, and defines the gap the present study addresses. First, the evidence base is overwhlemingly academic: argumentative essays, examination scripts, dissertations and researcha articles. Where L2 stance has been examined in non-academic settings, it has been in speech, where it varies systematically with task, medium and individual style [@GablasovaEtAl2017stance; @GablasovaEtAl2024]. I was unable to locate any established corpus study of L2 stance in informal online written registers, and lexical bundle research on informal online registers is limited to L1 data, notably Barbieri's [-@Barbieri2018] study of blogs and my own earlier analysis of BBC news comments [@Marchand2013]; the nearest other points of comparison are the conversation findings of the *Longman Grammar* [@BiberEtAl1999] and multidimensional, rather than bundle-based, analyses of web registers [@GrieveEtAl2010; @BiberEgbert2016]. Second, and consequently, it is unknown whether the calibration problems documented for academic writing are reproduced, attenuated, or transformed in a register such as ONC, whose communicative economy places a premium on direct evaluation and assertion rather than cautious qualification [CITATION and cf. chapter 2??]. If learners' stance habits reflect a mismatch with the academic register rather than a general deficit, then an informal evaluative register may reveal a substantially different learner profile, and only a comparison with native-speaker data from the same register can show which is the case. The next section turns to the specific population at the centre of that comparison, Japanese learners of English, and to what is known about their stance and phraseological behaviour.

# Japanese learners and sources of variation

The present section narrows the fouce from learner language in general to the population at the centre of this thesis: Japanese learners of English a a foreign language (EFL). The aim is not to characterise a homogenous "Japanese learner"; a construct that the critique of contrastive rhetoric has rendered untenable [@Kubota1999], but to do three more limited things: establish what corpus research has documented about this population, identify the explanations that compete whenever it is compared with native-speaker data, and assess how far findings drawn largely from argumentative essays and elicited speech extend to informal, online, evaluative discourse.

## Japanese learners in learner corpus research: a well-studied population

Japanese learners are among the most extensively studied EFL populations in learner corpus research, so I should be precise about the gap I address: it is not an absence of research but the restricted register base on which that research rests. The Japanese component of the International Corpus of Learner English (ICLE) placed Japanese university students' argumentative writing within the first large-sacle multinational learner corpus [@GrangerEtAl2009] and underpins early findings on connectors and pharseology discussed below [@Kaneko2007; @NaritaSatoSugiura2004]. At the school level, the Japanese EFL Learner (JEFLL) corpus comprises 10,038 short in-class compositions produced under controlled conditions (twenty minutes, no dicitonary, fixed topics) across the six years of Japanese secondary schooling, providing a quasi-longitudinal record of early instructed English development [@Tono2007]. At the university level, the International Corpus Network of Asian Learners of English (ICNALE) supplies written and spoken modules collected under strictly standardised conditions, with fixed prompts, proficiency information for every contributor, and matched native-speaker data (@Ishikawa2013; @Ishikawa2023]. Spoken proficiency is served by the NICT JLE Corpus of 1,281 rated oral proficiency interviews [@IzumiEtAl2004], and Miki's [-@Miki2010] work compares learner essays with their native-speaker corrections. Claims about Japanese learners can this in principle be tested against large, well-documented datasets spanning school and university, speech and writing, and beginner to advanced proficiency.

## Japanese learner proficiency and corpus research

A second well-developed strand concerns proficiency, which the major corpora operationalise differently, each solution carrying consequences for interpretation. ICNALE assigns writers to four bands linked to the Common European Framework of Reference for Languages (CEFR), but those bands are derived by converting heterogeneous external measures such as TOEFL, TOIEC and IELTS scores or the Vocabulary Size Test, so they are best described as CEFR-linked rather than independently rated [Ishikawa2013]. JEFLL exploits the near-universal start of English instruction in the first year of secondary schooling, so that school year functions as a coarse but clean proxt for instructional exposure [@Tono2007], while the NICT JLE corpus relies on trained ratings from a standardised speaking test [@IzumiEtAl2004]. Corpus-based developmental research on this population is correspondingly mature, beginning with Tono's [-@Tono2000] analysis of the acquisition order of English grammatical morphemes in Japanese learner writing. Extending to recent large-scale work, @Suzuki2024 analysed over a thousand learners across spoken and written corpora, and finds that the variety and frequency of epistemic stance devices increase with proficiency, but in a non-linear fashion complicated by the multifunctionality of the devices themselves.

The implication for the present thesis is that proficiency is a live alternative explanation for any difference between the learner and reference corpora in stance or phraseology. @Miki2010 shows that the overuse of *I think* diminishes across TOEIC bands, with advanced writers deploying the expression more selectively at points in persuasive prose where it marks the writer's position on a controversial issue. @Ishikawa2021 similarly reports a substantial gap between the vocabulary Japanese and other Asian learners are estimated to know (around 3,300 words on average) and the considerably smaller set they deploy in writing, constraining how any apparent phraseological restriction should be interpreted. The proficiency profile of the participants in the present study, and the procedures used to establish it, are accordingly treated as design variables in their own right and are described in Chapter 4.

## L1 Influence and contrastive rhetoric

The oldest and most contested explanation for distinctive features of Japanese learner writing is first language (L1) influence, and its intellectual home is contrastive rhetoric. @Kaplan1966 initiated the field with the claim that "Logic (in the popular, rather the logician's sense of the word) which is the basis of rhetoric, is evolved out of a culture; it is not universal" (p. 2). proposing patterns of paragraph development that are culture specific, including a famously indirect pattern attributed to "Oriental" writing. @Connor1996 consolidated this tradition into a research programme that sought to explain second-language composing difficulties by reference to the rhetorical strategies of the first language, and @Hinds1987 supplied its most influential claim as regards Japanese discourse: that Japanese prose is "reader-responsible", leaving interpretive work to the audience, in contrast to "writer-responsible" English. @Connor2002 subsequently repositioned the field as intercultural rhetoric, broadening its methods in response to the critiques.

These critiques, however, substantially qualify what contrastive rhetoric can license for the present study. @Kubota1997, [-@Kubota1999] showed empirically that direct, deductive organisational patterns coexist with inductive onew n Japanese expository writing, and argued that the image of a uniquely indirect Japanese rhetoric is a discourse construct rather than a descriptive fact. @KubotaLehner2004 and @Atkinson2004 generalised the objecti0on, contending that contrastive rhetoric has operated with static, essentialised cultural dichotomies that obscure variation within cultures, across genres and over time [see also @Leki1991]. Empirically, transfer itself appears partial rather than wholesale: @Kubota1998 found that Japanese university students carried some organisational features from L1 to L2 writing but by no means all. The constructive alternative is Matsuda's [-@Matsuda1997] dynamic model, in which L2 text feature emerge from the interaction of L1, proficiency, genre knowledge, instruction and individual variation. The position adopted in this thesis is accordingly a qualified one. Japanese L1 background is treated as one plausible explanatory factor among several, not as the first link in an inference from Japanese learners to Japanese rhetorical culture to distinctive stance phraseology; any putative L1 effect must survive comparison with the alternatives examined in Section 5.5, and the study's design, set out there and in Section 6.4, attempts to separate differences attributable to learner status from those attributable to register and other sources of variation.

## Japanese learners' discourse-pragmatic and stance choices

The evidence most directly relevant to this thesis concerns how Japanese learners deploy specific linguistic resources: hedging devices, assertive and self-mention devices, organsiational connectors, evalautive language and recurrent phraseological sequences. This subsection organises that evidence by resource rather than by study. Two things should be clarified here:  the evidence base consists almost entirely of argumentative essays and elicited speech, so it would be a stretch to generalise to other registers; the findings themselves admit several explanations, so they are reported here in descriptive terms, with interpretation to follow in Section 5.5.

### Hedging and epistemic modality

A recurring finding is a narrow epistemic repertoire (which is admitedly sometimes mismatched by register). @HollmannFujimotoKuroda2024 examined the modal verbs *may*, *might* and *could* in Japanese undergraduates' academic writing and found that *could* was used with high frequency, but often informally an insufficientlu in its epistemice-possibility sense; notably, their central interpretive frame is register, following Gilquin & Paquot's [-@GilquinPaquot2008] account of learner writing as "too chatty", rather than L1 influence. @Suzuki2024, applying a Systemic Functional Linguistics (SFL) value framework to spoken and written corpora, concurs with earlier studies that Japanese learners rely on epistemic adverbs and lexical verbs (such as *I think*, *I guess* and *maybe*) rather than modal verbs to realise epistemic modality, and that small repertoires concentrate on a few high-frequency items, especially at lower proficiency. @Pemberton2020, analysing a purpose-built corpus of 190 handwritten argumentative essays, adds two findings that complicate cultural explanations: the frequency of modal devices varied by topic, and learners used more hedges than boosters on every topic, a pattern that correlated with the school curriculum rather than any cultural variable. Taken together, these studies may suggest that Japanese learners hedge, but with a restricted inventory whose deployment is sensitive to topic, instruction and register rather than to culture alone.

### Boosting, direct assertion and writer visibility

Counter to the stereotype of the indirect, non-commital Japanese writer, several corpus studies report overuse of assertive and self-mention devices. @Kobayashi2016, comparing six L1 groups in ICNALE using a Hyland-style metadiscourse taxonomy [@Hyland2005??], found that Japanese learners used self-mentions, boosters, frame markers and attitude markers more frequently than other groups, explicitly against the prediction that writers from a "reader-responsible" language background should underuse such markers. The single most studied item is *I think*. @McCrostie2008 documents its overuse, particularly in sentence-initial position, in a corpus of over 300 Japanese university essays, and @Miki2010, using native-speaker corrections as the comparison baseline, confirms significant overuse across proficiency bands while cautioning against a purely transfered-based account. "Not all of the categorical misuses by the Japanese learners are due to L1 transfer; they are lacking in the knowledge of the proper uses of *I think*" (pp. 178-179). @Natsukari2012 adds a functional qualification, arguing that learners' *I think* is often closer in force to native-speaker *I believe*, a marker of committed stance rather than a hedge. The compostite picture is one of calibration rather than avoidance: stance is expressed, but sometimes at the wrong strength, in the wrong position or in the wrong register.

### Discourse organisation

The classic connector study is @NaritaSatoSugiura2004, who compared the ICLE Japanese subcorpus with LOCHNESS and found that Japanese learners "significantly oversue the logical connectors in sentence initial positions", overusing connectors such as *for example*, *of course* and *first*, while underusing *then*, *yet* and *instead* (p. 1174). Crucially for the question of competing questions, a parallel comparison with French, Swedish and Chinese learner data showed that the four groups share a common core of over- and underused connectors, with [L1-specific residue superimposed]??; the authors attribute the overuse largely to learners' incomplete grasp of the distinction between adverbial connectors and conjunctions, offering a developmental or instructional explanation rather than one derived from a cultural-rhetorical background. This pattern, in which an apparently Japanese feature turns out to be shared across L1 groups, recurs throughout this section, and is central to Section 5.5.

### Evaluation and interpersonal positioning

Evaluative and affective resources have been less extensively studied than modality, but the available evidence again resists the deficit-and-indirectness stereotype. @Kobayashi2016 reports overuse of attitude markers alongside boosters and self-mentions in Japanese ICNALE esssays, and @KamimuraOi1998 identified differences in argumentative strategies between American and Japanese students' English essays, including the use of generalisations and of *I think* as a softening rather than emphatic device, locating group differences in how evaluation is packaged rather than whether it is present. Evidence from informal online interaction remains extremely thin: @Matsuoka2021 reports that Japanese EFL learners in online forum discussion used a limited range of modal functions for social interaction, with certain pragmalinguistic norms appearing to have stabilised, but this is a small-scale conference study and, alongside my own work with Akutsu [CITATION], stands virtually alone as corpus evidence from an online register in Japan.

### Phraseology and recurrent sequences

Finally phraseological research suggests that Japanese recurrent sequences form a restricted repertoire that is partially distinctive due to L1. @Ishikawa2021, analysing trigrams in the ICNALE edited essays across four Asian L1 groups, found that learners overused sequences built around basic verbs, bare singular nouns an certain logical connectors, while underusing subjunctive and epistemic modal constuctions; of particular relevance here, Japanese learners were distinctive in their high-frequency trigram profiles. The most direct bundle-level evidence is @SitlerSpivey2025 multi-modal register analysis of four-word bundles across the ICNALE written essays and spoken monologues: Japanese learners relied on a larger proportion of verb-phrase-based bundles than the other groups, with a restricted range of bundle types and limited structural diversity in speech, and overall bundle frequency decreased as proficiency increased. Their title itself carries the alignment finding: *I agree with this* emerges as the dominant realisation of the first-person alignment frame in Japanese EFL argumentative writing, independently confirming the salience of a pattern this thesis pursues in the comment register. @Kaneko2007, in an early small-scale study of two- to four-word clusters in Japanese English majors' writing, likewise described a restricted repertoire in which a few function words combine around a core content word; given its scale, its findings are best treated as suggestive. Whether such repertoires persist in, or are reshaped by, informal evaluative registers is unknown, because the phraseological studies reviewed here and in Section 4 all concern academic or argumentative writing.

## L1, proficiency, task, register, topic and time as competing explanations

The studies reviewed above share a methodological vulnerability that matters directly for the design of the present thesis: each documents a difference between Japanese learner output and some native-speaker baseline, yet the explanations on offer are rarely pitted against one another within a single design. This subsection therefore confronts the inferential question on which the whole thesis turns: if the learner corpus differs from the reference corpus, what may legitimately be inferred from the difference? To make the problem concrete, return to the hypothetical finding introduced in Section 1.2: a hedged evaluative frame, characteristic of native-speaker comment discourse, that is markedly less frequent in the Japanese learners' comments than in the BBC *Have Your Say* reference corpus. At least six explanations are available, each with prima facie support in the literature reviewed in this chapter.

First, **L1 influence**: the function the bundle serves in English comment discourse may be realised by different rhetorical means in Japanese, and learners may transfer those means, or avoid the function altogether [@Connor1996]. Against this, transfer has repeatedly shown to be partial [@Kubota1998], and patterns attributed to Japanese rhetoric have turned out to be shared across unrelated L1 groups [@NaritaSatoSugiura2004] [PLUS more  CITATIONS SUPPORTING TRANSFER]?. Second, **proficiency**: the bundle may simply be beyond the learners' current repertoire, since epistemic and phraseological repertoires expand, non-linearly, with proficiency [@Ishikawa2021; @Suzuki2024], and even robust overuses such as *I think* attenuate across proficiency bands [@Miki2010]. Third, **task**: the conditions under which the comments were produced, whether timed or untimed, prompted or spontaneous, individually written or classroom-assigned, measurably alter linguistic output [@WayJoinerSeaman2000], and the learners' production conditions almost certainly differed from those of the native commenters. Fourth, **register**: the learners may be producing a different register from the reference corpus, or an informalised version of the target register; learner writing is pervasively "too chatty" [@GilquinPaquot2008], and Japanese learners' epistemic choices in particular have been characterised as register-inappropriate rather than ungrammatical [@HollmannFujimotoKuroda2024]. Fifth, **topic**: stance and modality frequencies vary with subject matter, as @Pemberton2020 demonstrates directly for Japanese learners, whose modal usage tracked topic and curriculum rather than culture, and as topic effects on syntactic and lexical measurees confirm more generally [@YangLuWeigle2015]. Sixth, **time**: the two corpora differ in their period of data collection, and registers are not static. The BBC comments date from the early 2000s, and some part of any difference between the corpora may reflect diachronic drift in the register itself, or in the wider ecology of online discourse, rather than any property of the learners.

Larsson, Paquot and Biber's [-@LarssonPaquotBiber2021] study is again instructive here: beyond establishing that register is a major source of variation in learner writing (Section 3.3), their multidimensional analysis modelled L1 background and register as co-predictors across five L1 groups and multiple written registers. Their demonstration that significant differences emerge both between writer groups and across registers implies that, for Japanese learners, register cannot simply be acknowledged and set aside: it must be actively disentangled from L1 and proficiency. Concretely, an L1 account requires evidence that the effect is specific to Japanese learners relative to other L1 groups of comparable proficiency writing in the same register; a proficiency account requires that bundle use vary with proficiency within the Japanese sample; task and topic accounts require comparisons across tasks and topics; and ruling register in or out requires, at minimum, that the learner and reference corpora represent the same register, as the comparability principle requires (Section 2.4), supplemented where possible by situating both corpora among a wider range of native-speaker registers. A time-based explanation, finally, is mitigated by treating the BBC data explicitly as a benchmark of the register at a defined historical moment, rather than as a timeless native norm. ICNALE's design, with fixed prompts, controlled conditions and proficiency bands for ten Asian L1 groups [@Ishikawa2013], shows what such disentangling looks like for argumentative writing; and the proof-of-concept study for this thesis applied precisely that design, modelling sparse evaluative bundle frequencies in ICNALE Japanese and native-speaker essays with Poisson pseudo-maximum likelihood and reading proficiency trajectories against the native benchmark [-@marchand2026]; no equivalent design exists for informal online evaluative discourse. Table 3.4 summarises the six explanations and the evidence that would discriminate among them.

**Table 3.4**

*Competing explanations for a hypothetical underuse of a stance bundle by Japanese learners, with discriminating evidence*

| Explanation | Account of the underuse | Evidence that would support it |
|---|---|---|
| L1 influence | Function realised differently in Japanese rhetoric; transfer or avoidance | Effect specific to Japanese learners vs. other L1 groups at comparable proficiency in the same register [cf. @Connor1996; @Kubota1998] |
| Proficiency | Bundle beyond current repertoire | Frequency/functional range varies with proficiency within the Japanese sample [cf. @Miki2010; @Suzuki2024] |
| Task | Production conditions suppress or licence the bundle | Bundle use varies with timing, prompting and setting for the same writers [cf. @WayJoinerSeaman2000] |
| Register | Learners produce a different or informalised register | Learner corpus patterns with informal registers on register-sensitive features [cf. @GilquinPaquot2008; @LarssonPaquotBiber2021] |
| Topic | Subject matter conditions stance choices | Bundle use varies by topic within each population [cf. @Pemberton2020; @YangLuWeigle2015] |
| Time | Register drift between data-collection periods | BBC data treated as a benchmark of the register at a defined historical moment, not a timeless native norm (see 3.3.3) |

None of the six explanations can be privileged *a priori*, and they are not mututally exclusive: Matsuda's [-@Matsuda1997] dynamic model anticipated precisely this kind of multi-causal interaction. What the hypothetical demonstrates is that a raw difference in frequency between the learner and reference corpora, of the kind a corpus comparison of online news comments will inevitably produce, is uninformative until L1, proficiency, task, register, topic and time have been systematically considered. The principle that governs all interpretation in the chapters ahead can therefore be stated plainly. A difference between learner and native-speaker usage is not, in itself, evidence of L1 transfer.

## Synthesis

Japanese learners of English are among the most extensively studied EFL populations in learner corpus research, supported by large, well-documented resources spanning school and university, speech and writing, and multiple proficiecny levels [@GrangerEtAl2009; @Ishikawa2013; @IzumiEtAl2004; @Tono2007]. This research has documented differences, relative to native-speaker norms, in vocabulary development, grammatical development, discourse organisation, stance marking and phraseological patterning; crucially, the strongest studies simultaneously supply the counter-evidence that undermines single-cause accounts: connector overuse is shared across L1 groups [@NaritaSatoSugiura2004], modality tracks topic and curriculum rather than culture [@Pemberton2020], *I think* overuse reflects incomplete register knowledge as much as transfer [@Miki2010], and Japanese learners tend to overuse, rather than avoid, assertive and self-mention devices [@Kobayashi2016]. The contrastive-rhetoric tradition that once offered a deterministic cultural explanation for such findings has been thoroughly qualified [@Atkinson2004; @Kubota1997; @Kubota1999; @KubotaLehner2004], leaving L1 as one influence among many [@Matsuda1997]. The pervasive limitation is one of register coverage: virtually everything known about this population comes from argumentative essays, examination conditions  or elicited speech, and Japan-specific evidence from informal online interaction remains confined to a handful of small-scale studies [@Matsuoka2021]. Whether the patterns documented in academic and controlled writing extend to informal, online, evaluative discourse, are attenuated there, or are transforemed, remains unclear.

# Synthesis: From learner corpus research to learner stance in ONC

## What this chapter has established: a chain of propositions

The argument of this chapter can now be stated as a chain of six propositions, each defended in the preceding sections and each a premise fot the next.

First, learner corpus research (LCR) establishes the value of systematically comparing learner and native-speaker production. By comparing large bodies of learner production with native-speaker production, Contrastive Interlanguage Analysis (CIA) makes visible quantitative divergences, the overuse and underuse of perfectly well-formed items, that error analysis was structurally unable to detect [@Granger1996; @Granger1998book]. Seconc, CIA shows that such comparison is only as strong as its reference population: the native corpus is a sample of what a defined community of users does in a defined situation, not an idealised targer [@Granger2015; @Gilquin2022], which is why the BBC *Have Your Say* corpus functions in this thesis as a register-specific benchmark rather than a prescriptive model. Third, register research shows that learner production varies substantially with communicative context. Multidimensional studies repeatedly find register and tasks effects of the same order as, or larger than, proficiency and first langauge (L1) effects [@GardnerNesiBiber2019; @LarssonPaquotBiber2021; @StaplesReppen2016], and learners themselves show partial but real register awareness [@LarssonKaatari2020; @QinUccelli2020]. Fourth, L2 stance research shows systematic differences between learner and native-speaker writing in interpersonal and epistemic resources, differences located in the calibration of commitment rather than its quantity: restricted repertoires, stronger and less precisely graded claims, and simultaneous over- and under-marking [@HylandMilton1997; @Adel2006; @AullLancaster2014]. Fifth, phraseological research shows that these differences extend to recurrent multiword sequences: learners command narrower and structurally different bundle repertoires whose composition varies with proficiency and register [@ChenBaker2010; @ChenBaker2016; @AdelErman2012; @BiberBarbieri2007]. Sixth, Japanese learner research identifies L1 and proficiency relevant, competing sources of variation, and repeatedly demonstrates that apparently L1-specific features are shared across unrelated L1 groups, attenuate with proficiency, or track topic and curriculum rather than culture [@Miki2010; @NaritaSatoSugiura2004; @Pemberton2020].

Taken together, the six propositions yield this chapter's central conclusion. Every explanation available for differences between learner and native-speaker stance phraseology, whether transfer, proficiency, task or topic, is sensitive to register, and register effects are independently large. Register therefore cannot be treated as a background variable when interpreting such differences: it is a constitutive condition of their interpretation.

## The double gap

The conclusion of Chapter 2 and the conclusion of the present chapter intersect. Chapter 2 identified a register gap: the phraseological realisation of stance in online news commenting is not adequately understood, and no systematic account exists of how native-speaker commenters habitually express evaluation, commitment and reader orientation through recurrent sequences. The present chapter establishes a learner-context gap: research on L2 stance and stance phraseology, including the extensive work on Japanese learners [@Ishikawa2013; @Ishikawa2023; @Tono2007], has concentrated on academic or otherwise controlled writing, so that findings from those registers cannot be assumed to generalise to informal online evaluation. The thesis addresses the intersection of the two gaps, asking how Japanese learners realise stance phraseologically when producing in the ONC register. Stated as a single problem: *the phraseological realisation of stance by Japanese learners in an informal evaluative online register has not been adequately investigated.* Investigating it requires addessing both gaps at once, since a register-aware description of native ONC stance phraseology is the benchmark against which learner usage becomes interpretable at all.

## Methodological implications for Chapter 4

The double gap translates into six explicit requirements that the design reported in Chapter 4 must satisfy.

1. **Register comparability.** Because register effects can rival or exceed the effects of learner status [@LarssonPaquotBiber2021], the learner and reference corpora must represent the same broad register. The comparison is accordingly between Japanese learners' online news comments and native-speaker online news comments, not between learner comments and native academic or journalistic prose.
2. **Task comparability** Production condition shape linguistic output independently of register [@Granger1996]. The communicative conditions under which the learner comments were produced must therefore be documented and, where possible, rendered comparable to those of the native data, with residual differences acknowledged rather than concealed.
3. **Learner comparability.** Since L1 and proficiency are live competing explanations [@Miki2010; @Suzuki2024], the learner corpus must have both variables fully documented, so that both can be controlled and examined rather than assumed.
4. **An appropriate reference population.** Consistent with CIA2 [@Granger2015; @Gilquin2022], the BBC *Have Your Say* corpus serves as a benchmark from the same register (Section 2.3.3), not as an abstract native-English model.
5. **Phraseological analysis.** Because learners differ from native-speaker writers in recurrent combinations and not only in isolated items [@ChenBaker2010; @AdelErman2012], the analysis must capture recurrent multi-word sequences rather than relying on counts of individual stance markers alone.
6. **Functional interpretation.** Frequency differences are evidentially inert until interpreted against discourse function [cf. @HylandMilton1997; @ChenBaker2016]: overuse or underuse of a form must be read in terms of what the form does in ONC, and raw counts alone cannot decide among the competing explanations reviewed in Section 5.

These requirements jointly operationalise the comparability principle set out in Section 2.4.

## From review to research design

The three bodies of research reviewed in this chapter supply the components of the required response: learner corpus research the comparative framework and its interpretive cautions, register research the situational controls, and stance and phraseology research the analytical level at which differences between learner and native-speaker evaluation and epistemic commitment become visible. They are individually well developed, but they have not been jointly applied to informal, evaluative online discourse produced by Japanese learners. Chapter 4 describes the corpora and analytical design through which this thesis does so: it details the construction of the six-cohort learner corpus and the BBC *Have Your Say* reference corpus, and it sets out a two-stage analysis combining an additive multidimensional analysis (MDA), which situates both corpora among a wider range of native-speaker registers, with the identification of stance-related phraseological patterns, recurrent sequences defined over tagged stance features such as evaluative adjectives, stance adverbs, suasive verbs and private verbs, and their lexical realisations as bundles.
